sla_notes_intro: Music is the art of organising sounds and silence in time to express ideas and emotions, and its scope covers many elements, functions and links with other fields.
sla_notes_details: Music is organised sound. Its main elements are rhythm (pattern of long and short sounds), melody (a succession of pitches), harmony (sounds played together), dynamics (loudness and softness), tempo (speed), timbre (tone colour), texture and form. Functions of music include entertainment, education, worship, communication, preserving culture, expressing feelings, healing, work coordination, ceremonies and political mobilisation. Music is important for national identity, employment and social unity. It relates to other fields such as mathematics (rhythm and time values), physics (sound and vibration), language and literature (lyrics), history, dance and drama, and technology.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a wedding song uses rhythm and melody to entertain, and its lyrics advise the couple, showing music serving both entertainment and education.
sla_notes_daily_life: People use music at home, in worship, at school, in ceremonies, in advertising and for relaxation.
sla_exercise: Define music.::The art of organising sound and silence in time to express ideas and feelings.||Name three elements of music.::Rhythm, melody and harmony (also dynamics, tempo or timbre).||State two functions of music in society.::Entertainment and education (also worship, preserving culture).

sla_notes_intro: Grade I theory introduces the basic tools of notation: rhythm, the stave and clefs, pitch names, simple intervals and common musical terms and signs.
sla_notes_details: Rhythm: note values are the semibreve (4 beats), minim (2), crotchet (1) and quaver (half), with equivalent rests; dotted notes add half their value; time signatures 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 show the number and type of beats in a bar. Staff notation: five lines and four spaces; the treble clef and bass clef; note names A to G; ledger lines; middle C. Melody and harmony: the major scales of C, G and F and the natural notes; the tonic triad; the interval of a 2nd to 5th by number. Terms and signs: forte (f), piano (p), crescendo, diminuendo, allegro, andante, adagio, legato, staccato, tie, slur, repeat marks and the pause sign. Learners write scales and short rhythms and identify notes on the staff.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in 4/4 time a bar may contain a minim, a crotchet and two quavers, since 2 + 1 + 0.5 + 0.5 equals 4 beats.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding notation helps singers and instrumentalists in choirs and bands to read and play music accurately.
sla_exercise: How many crotchet beats are in a semibreve?::Four.||What does the sign p (piano) mean?::Soft.||Name the notes on the spaces of the treble clef.::F, A, C and E.

sla_notes_intro: Singing simple melodies requires correct posture, breathing, pitch and clear pronunciation, whether one sings alone or in a group.
sla_notes_details: Good singing starts with a relaxed upright posture, deep diaphragmatic breathing, an open mouth and clear diction. Learners do vocal warm-ups such as humming, lip trills and sirens, then sing simple tunes in a comfortable range, matching the pitch given by an instrument or teacher. Solo singing develops confidence and personal expression; unison group singing develops blend, balance and listening skills, and the ability to follow a conductor. Voices are classified as soprano, alto, tenor and bass. Learners perform songs in Kiswahili and foreign languages, taking care of tempo and dynamics.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the class sings a simple folk melody in unison, then individual students sing a verse alone while others hum softly.
sla_notes_daily_life: People sing in church choirs, school assemblies, weddings and community events, using the skills of breathing and pitch.
sla_exercise: Name the four main voice types.::Soprano, alto, tenor and bass.||Why should a singer breathe from the diaphragm?::To have enough breath support for steady tone and long phrases.||What is unison singing?::Singing the same melody at the same pitch together.

sla_notes_intro: Local percussion instruments produce sound when struck, shaken or scraped and are used to provide rhythm for songs.
sla_notes_details: Common Tanzanian percussion instruments include ngoma (drums of various sizes), marimba or ilimba, shakers such as njuga or mikwaju, rattles, castanets, wooden sticks and clappers. Learners study how to hold them, the correct striking positions, and how to play steady beats, patterns and simple ostinatos. Accompaniment supports the singer with a steady pulse, matching tempo and dynamics without covering the voice. Care of instruments includes keeping drums dry, checking the skin and storing shakers safely.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, one group plays a steady pulse on a ngoma while another plays a short repeating rhythm on shakers as the class sings a simple melody.
sla_notes_daily_life: Percussion accompanies songs at traditional ceremonies, church services, weddings and school events.
sla_exercise: Name two local percussion instruments.::Ngoma and shakers (also marimba, rattles).||What is the role of percussion in accompaniment?::It provides the beat and rhythmic support for the song.||How should a drum be cared for?::Keep it dry and clean and avoid overheating or damaging the skin.

sla_notes_intro: Grade II theory builds on Grade I by adding new note values, time signatures, keys and intervals.
sla_notes_details: Rhythm: semiquavers and their rests, dotted crotchets, triplets in simple cases and the time signatures 2/4, 3/4, 4/4 and additional 6/8 in some settings. Staff notation: the treble and bass clefs with ledger lines; sharps, flats and naturals; tones and semitones. Melody and harmony: major scales C, G, D, A and F and the minor scale of A, D and E with key signatures; degrees of the scale by number; intervals by number; the tonic, subdominant and dominant triads. Terms and signs: moderato, allegretto, rit., a tempo, mezzo forte, accent, tenuto, da capo, fine and simple ornaments. Learners write scales, transpose short tunes and analyse simple melodies.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the key signature of G major has one sharp, F sharp, so every F in the piece is played as F sharp unless cancelled.
sla_notes_daily_life: Reading notation helps choir members and instrumentalists to learn new songs independently.
sla_exercise: How many sharps has the key of D major?::Two (F sharp and C sharp).||What does rit. mean?::Gradually slower (ritardando).||How many semiquavers equal one crotchet?::Four.

sla_name: Theories of the existence and source of musical sounds
sla_assessment_criteria: Theories related to the existence/ source of musical sounds are explained clearly.
sla_teaching_aids: Piano|Guitar|Ngoma|Audio|Video clips of various musical|Non-musical sounds
sla_references: TET(2023), MUSIC SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Various theories explain the origin of music and how musical sounds are produced, including the classification of instruments.
sla_notes_details: Origin theories include the divine origin (music is a gift from God or ancestors), the imitation of nature (sounds of birds, wind and water inspired music), the work and rhythm theory (labour chants coordinated work), the speech and language theory (music grew out of tonal speech and emotional cries) and the ritual and social theory. Musical sounds come from vibrating bodies such as strings, air columns, membranes and solid bodies. Instruments are classified as chordophones (strings, e.g. zeze, guitar), aerophones (wind, e.g. filimbi, trumpet), membranophones (skin, e.g. ngoma) and idiophones (self-sounding, e.g. marimba, shaker), and electrophones (electronic, e.g. keyboard). This is the Hornbostel-Sachs system.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a zeze produces sound when a string vibrates, so it is a chordophone, while a shaker sounds by its own body vibrating, so it is an idiophone.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowing how instruments produce sound helps musicians choose and care for instruments and understand the sounds around them.
sla_exercise: Which instrument family does the ngoma belong to?::Membranophones.||Name one theory of the origin of music.::The imitation of nature theory (or work and rhythm theory, divine origin theory).||Classify the guitar.::A chordophone (string instrument).

sla_teaching_aids: Piano|Guitar|Ngoma|Music scores|Music sheets
sla_references: TET(2023), MUSIC SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Composing is creating original melodies and lyrics that follow musical rules and express a clear message.
sla_notes_details: Steps of composition are: select a theme (for example environment, health or unity); write lyrics in Kiswahili with a clear structure of verses and chorus; choose a key and time signature; create a melody that fits the natural stress of the words; keep phrases balanced (4 or 8 bars); use repetition and contrast; end on the tonic; write the tune on the staff or in tonic sol-fa; and add dynamics and tempo marks. ICT tools such as notation software and recording apps may help. Compositions should respect Tanzanian culture and language and avoid copying other people's work.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a learner writes a four-line chorus in Kiswahili encouraging cleanliness, sets it in C major in 4/4 time and ends the melody on the note C.
sla_notes_daily_life: Songs are composed for school events, campaigns, worship and advertisements to pass messages.
sla_exercise: State two steps in composing a song.::Choosing a theme and writing lyrics, then creating a melody to fit the words.||On which note does a melody in C major normally end?::On C, the tonic.||Why should the melody fit the natural stress of words?::So that the lyrics sound natural and are easily understood.

sla_notes_intro: Singing short songs develops accuracy of pitch and rhythm, expression and teamwork.
sla_notes_details: Learners practise breath control, correct diction and interpretation of dynamics, phrasing and tempo. In solo singing, they memorise the song, maintain pitch without accompaniment and communicate the meaning. In group singing, they blend voices, listen to others, follow the conductor's gestures and start and stop together. Snow-balling is used: one student sings, then more join. Learners perform in Kiswahili and other languages and evaluate one another on pitch, rhythm, expression and stage presence.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, one learner starts a short song, then a second group joins on the chorus, and finally the whole class sings while following the teacher's conducting.
sla_notes_daily_life: Skills are used in school choirs, church services, family gatherings and public celebrations.
sla_exercise: What should singers do to blend as a group?::Listen to each other and match volume and tone.||Give one thing a soloist must do while performing.::Maintain correct pitch and rhythm and express the meaning of the song.||Why is a conductor's gesture important?::It helps singers start, stop and keep tempo and dynamics together.

sla_notes_intro: Foreign percussion instruments include those from other countries or the orchestra, and they can accompany short songs.
sla_notes_details: Examples are the snare drum, bass drum, tambourine, triangle, cymbals, bongos, congas, timpani, xylophone, glockenspiel and drum kit. Learners study their construction, playing techniques (striking, rolling, shaking and damping) and the roles they play in a band, such as keeping a beat and adding colour. Accompaniment patterns like a steady four-beat pulse or a march rhythm are practised using scores and sheets, while the player follows the singer and controls volume. Tuned percussion such as the glockenspiel can also play the melody.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a tambourine playing on beats 2 and 4 with a triangle on beat 1 provides a light accompaniment to a short song in 4/4.
sla_notes_daily_life: Percussion appears in school bands, brass bands, church bands and popular music groups.
sla_exercise: Name two foreign percussion instruments.::Snare drum and tambourine (also triangle, cymbals, xylophone).||Which foreign percussion instruments are tuned?::Glockenspiel and xylophone (also timpani).||What should a percussionist avoid when accompanying a singer?::Playing so loudly that the singer cannot be heard.

sla_notes_intro: A music recording studio is a specially designed space where sounds are captured, edited and mixed to produce recorded music.
sla_notes_details: A studio has a live room where musicians perform, a control room where the engineer works, and isolation booths for vocals. It is acoustically treated with soundproofing, absorbing panels and diffusers to reduce noise and echo. Key people include the producer, sound engineer, session musicians and artist. Stages of production are recording, editing, mixing and mastering. Modern studios use computers running a digital audio workstation (DAW). Safe and quiet studio behaviour and good time management are expected.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a singer stands in the vocal booth with a pop filter and headphones while the engineer records from the control room.
sla_notes_daily_life: Music studios in towns record songs, jingles, radio adverts and gospel albums, and offer employment to young people.
sla_exercise: Name the two main rooms in a studio.::The live (recording) room and the control room.||Why is a studio soundproofed and acoustically treated?::To keep out unwanted noise and prevent echo and reflections.||Name the stages of production.::Recording, editing, mixing and mastering.

sla_notes_intro: Recording equipment captures, processes and reproduces sound.
sla_notes_details: Main equipment includes microphones (dynamic and condenser) to convert sound to electrical signals, microphone stands and pop filters, audio interface converting analogue to digital signals, computer with a DAW such as FL Studio, Cubase, Pro Tools or Audacity, mixing console, studio monitors (speakers) and headphones, MIDI keyboard or controller, cables (XLR, jack, USB), amplifiers, and effects processors. sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a condenser microphone is used for vocals because it captures fine detail, while a dynamic microphone is used for loud drums.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowledge of equipment is useful to church media teams, school clubs and small studio owners.

learning_activity_name: Describe the fundamentals of reading and writing music based on ABRSM Music Theory Grade III (Rhythm, staff notation, melody and harmony, and musical terms and signs)
sla_name: Fundamentals of reading and writing music: ABRSM Grade III
sla_method: ICT- based learning and Case Study

sla_teaching_aids: ABRSM music theory guideline|Music scores|Music sheets|Piano|Guitar|Ngoma
sla_references: TET(2023), MUSIC SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Grade III theory extends notation to compound time, more keys, and wider intervals and terms.
sla_notes_details: Rhythm: compound time signatures 6/8 (two dotted-crotchet beats), and simple times 2/4, 3/4, 4/4 and 2/2 or 3/8; triplets, dotted rhythms and rests; anacrusis (upbeat). Staff notation: the treble and bass clefs with ledger lines; key signatures up to three sharps or flats (major C, G, D, A, F, B flat, E flat; minor A, E, B, D, G, C). Melody and harmony: major and minor scales (natural, harmonic and melodic); scale degrees and technical names (tonic, supertonic, mediant, subdominant, dominant, submediant, leading note); intervals by number and quality (major, minor, perfect); triads I, IV and V and chords in root position. Terms and signs: vivace, largo, con brio, dolce, sforzando, molto, poco, D.S., coda, and ornaments such as the trill. Learners transpose short melodies and write scales with correct accidentals.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the key of B flat major has two flats (B flat and E flat), and its dominant chord is F, A and C.
sla_notes_daily_life: Reading and writing notation helps choir directors and band members to arrange and share music.
sla_exercise: How many beats per bar are felt in 6/8 time?::Two (dotted crotchet beats).||Name the technical name of the fifth degree of a scale.::The dominant.||How many flats has the key of F major?::One (B flat).

sla_references: TET(2023), MUSIC SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Different Tanzanian communities explain the existence and role of music through their traditions, beliefs and daily life.
sla_notes_details: Many communities believe music originated from ancestors and the spirit world and is used in rituals, initiation, healing and worship. Other explanations link music with work such as farming, fishing and pastoralism, where songs coordinate labour, and with rites of passage such as birth, initiation, marriage and death. Examples include the Sukuma dance societies (Bagalu and Bagika), Gogo and Maasai songs, Makonde ngoma, Chagga folk songs and coastal taarab. Music is passed on orally and by participation, teaching history, values and identity. Modern Tanzanian music, such as bongo flava, developed by blending traditional, foreign and popular influences.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the Gogo sing work songs during cultivation to keep rhythm and reduce fatigue, while the Makonde perform ngoma at initiation ceremonies.
sla_notes_daily_life: Tanzanians use music at weddings, funerals, festivals and national celebrations, keeping cultural identity alive.
sla_exercise: Name one Tanzanian community and its type of music.::Makonde and their ngoma (or Sukuma and their society dances).||Why are work songs sung?::To coordinate work, keep rhythm and reduce tiredness.||Name a modern Tanzanian music style.::Bongo flava (or taarab).

sla_notes_intro: Two-part harmony combines two independent vocal lines that sound together and fit the harmony of the song.
sla_notes_details: Learners compose short English lyrics on a chosen theme, then write a melody for the upper voice in a major key. The second part is created below the melody, usually in thirds or sixths, moving mostly in parallel with occasional contrary motion, and using notes of the chords I, IV and V. Avoid parallel fifths and octaves and unnecessary large leaps. The parts start together, end on the tonic and have well-balanced phrases. Both lines are written on the stave with clear notation, key signature, time signature, dynamics and tempo. Software may be used to play back the harmony.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, if the melody is C-D-E-C, a lower part in thirds may be A-B-C-A, which fits with the C major harmony.
sla_notes_daily_life: Two-part songs are sung by school choirs and youth groups at concerts and worship.
sla_exercise: What is two-part harmony?::Two different vocal lines sung together to make harmony.||Which intervals are commonly used between the two parts?::Thirds and sixths.||On which note do the parts usually end?::The tonic (key note).

sla_notes_intro: Singing in two parts requires each singer to hold their own line while listening to the other part.
sla_notes_details: Learners are divided into upper and lower voices. The teacher first teaches each part separately, then combines them slowly. Techniques include tuning to a reference pitch, breathing together, singing in tune with other parts, maintaining balance so neither part dominates and following the conductor. Snow-balling is used to build confidence, first pairs then larger groups. Learners evaluate accuracy of pitch, rhythm and blend, and record and replay their performance.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, sopranos sing the melody while altos sing a third below, and both parts join on the final chord.
sla_notes_daily_life: Two-part singing is used in choirs and church groups and improves listening skills.
sla_exercise: What should singers do to hold their own part?::Listen to their own line, use a reference pitch and not follow the other part.||Name two voice groups used in two-part singing.::Soprano and alto (or tenor and bass).||Why are parts first practised separately?::So each singer learns the line accurately before combining.

sla_notes_intro: String instruments produce sound by vibrating strings that are plucked, bowed or strummed, and they can support songs with chords and melodies.
sla_notes_details: Local string instruments include the zeze (bowed or plucked), ndono, kinanda, ngoma-lute (nanga) and the fiddle; foreign ones include guitar, violin, cello, double bass, mandolin and harp. Learners study the parts of the instrument, tuning, holding position, right and left hand techniques, and simple chords such as C, G and F on guitar or open strings on the zeze. Accompaniment patterns include strumming, arpeggios and a steady bass line. The player follows the tempo of the singer and keeps the instrument in tune and clean.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a guitarist accompanying a song in C major strums chords C, F and G to provide harmony.
sla_notes_daily_life: String instruments are common in taarab bands, church groups, and folk music, and are also played at family parties.

sla_notes_intro: Ethics are principles of right conduct, and norms and values guide artists, producers and audiences in the music industry.
sla_notes_details: The industry is regulated by BASATA (National Arts Council), COSOTA (Copyright Society of Tanzania) and the Tanzania Film Board and the Ministry responsible for arts. Ethical principles include respect for copyright, honesty in contracts, avoiding plagiarism, respect for culture and moral values in lyrics, protection of children, fair payments and royalties, avoiding drugs and violence, punctuality, professionalism and respect for fellow artists and audiences. Breaking ethics results in lawsuits, bans, public rejection and loss of income. Registered artists and promoters are expected to follow the regulations.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, an artist who samples someone else's beat without permission violates copyright and may face legal action.
sla_notes_daily_life: Good conduct by musicians serves as a role model to young people and builds trust with the public.
sla_exercise: Name two organisations that regulate music in Tanzania.::BASATA and COSOTA.||Give one ethical rule for musicians.::Respect copyright and do not plagiarise (or write lyrics that respect culture).||What may happen to an artist who breaks the rules?::Legal action, a ban or loss of reputation.

sla_notes_intro: Music notation software allows composers to write, edit, play back and print scores on a computer or phone.
sla_notes_details: Examples are MuseScore, Sibelius, Finale, Noteflight and Flat.io. Features include note entry by mouse, keyboard or MIDI keyboard, playback, transposition, part extraction, printing and export to PDF or audio. Advantages: neat, error-free scores, easy correction, quick sharing and playback of a piece without an instrument. Limitations are dependence on power and computers, and the need for skill and software licences. Learners identify the interface, toolbars, palettes and the differences between free and commercial programs.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in MuseScore a user chooses a treble clef and time signature, then clicks the stave to add notes and presses play to hear the melody.
sla_notes_daily_life: Composers, teachers and choir directors use notation software to prepare scores and teaching materials quickly.
sla_exercise: Name two music notation programs.::MuseScore and Sibelius (also Finale, Noteflight).||State one advantage of notation software.::It plays back the music and gives neat printed scores.||Which type of file can be used to share a score as a document?::A PDF file.

sla_notes_intro: Learners use notation software to enter, edit and play back a short melody on one stave.
sla_notes_details: Steps: open the program and create a new score for a single instrument or voice; choose the key signature, time signature and tempo; select the note duration then click the note position on the stave or use a keyboard; add rests, ties, dynamics and lyrics; use the playback button to check; correct errors; save the file and print or export it. Learners must check that every bar has the correct number of beats, and that the melody matches the lyrics.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a learner enters an eight-bar melody in G major 4/4, adds the lyrics under the notes and exports a PDF.
sla_notes_daily_life: The skill helps a young musician prepare songs for a choir or a school concert.

sla_notes_intro: Recording procedures are the ordered steps followed to record and produce a song in a studio.
sla_notes_details: Steps: pre-production (planning the song, arrangement, choosing the studio, booking time), setting up (equipment, microphone placement, headphones, levels and a sound check), tracking (recording rhythm section, then instruments and vocals, often in multiple takes), editing (choosing the best takes, correcting timing and pitch), mixing (balancing levels, panning, EQ, effects such as reverb and compression), mastering (final polish for loudness and consistency across platforms) and distribution. A DAW records each instrument on separate tracks. Good file naming and back-ups are important.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after recording a vocal on one track, the engineer adds reverb and balances it against the guitar during mixing.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowing the steps helps young artists plan a recording and work well with producers.
sla_exercise: What happens during mixing?::The levels, panning and effects of the tracks are balanced.||Which step is done after mixing?::Mastering.||Why should recordings be backed up?::To avoid losing the work if a device fails.

sla_notes_intro: Copyright is the legal right of creators to control the use and earn from their original works.
sla_notes_details: In Tanzania, the Copyright and Neighbouring Rights Act protects musical works, lyrics and recordings. The copyright owner has exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, perform in public, broadcast and adapt the work, and moral rights to be named. Protection lasts for the author's life plus fifty years (as provided by the Act). COSOTA administers rights, collects royalties and registers works. Infringement includes piracy, unauthorised sampling and public use without permission or payment. Penalties include fines, imprisonment and damages. Fair use allows limited use for education or review.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a radio station playing an artist's songs pays royalties collected by COSOTA and shared with the artists.
sla_notes_daily_life: Buying original music instead of pirated copies supports artists and their livelihood.
sla_exercise: What is copyright?::The legal right of creators to control and benefit from their original works.||Which organisation administers copyright in music in Tanzania?::COSOTA.||Give one example of copyright infringement.::Copying and selling a song without the owner's permission (piracy).

sla_notes_intro: Archiving means storing music in an organised, safe way for future access, while respecting the rights of the owners.
sla_notes_details: Learners save recordings and scores in digital formats such as MP3, WAV, PDF and notation-software files, using clear file names (title, composer, date), folders by type, and metadata such as artist, year and genre. Back-ups are kept on external drives, flash disks and cloud storage. Passwords and permissions protect the files. Each work stored includes a note on the copyright owner and the permission for use. Learners include only their own compositions or works with permission, register works with COSOTA and avoid uploading pirated content.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a learner creates a folder named School Songs 2026 with sub-folders Audio and Scores, and each file name shows the title and composer.
sla_notes_daily_life: Choirs and schools keep archives of their songs to preserve heritage and prepare for future events.
sla_exercise: Name two file formats used for storing music.::MP3 and WAV (also PDF for scores).||Why is a back-up necessary?::To avoid losing works if the main storage is damaged.||What should be recorded about each archived song?::Title, composer/owner, date and permission for use.

sla_notes_details: Platforms include YouTube, Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, X (Twitter), WhatsApp and streaming apps such as Boomplay and Audiomack. Promotional methods include posting short clips, lyric videos, behind-the-scenes content, live sessions, hashtags, collaborations with other artists, engaging with fans, and announcing events. Good practice: use quality audio, regular posting, consistent branding, respect for copyright and community rules, and protecting personal information. Analytics show viewers and help plan. Dangers include cyberbullying, false information and time wasting.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a student posts a 30-second clip of an original chorus on TikTok with a hashtag and answers comments from listeners.

sla_notes_intro: A research project investigates a question about music business opportunities using systematic data collection.
sla_notes_details: Music business opportunities include performing, recording and production, teaching, instrument making and repair, composing for adverts and films, event management, DJ and sound services, music publishing, streaming, merchandising and copyright administration. Steps of research: choose a topic and objectives, review cases of successful ventures, design instruments (questionnaire, interview, observation), collect data from artists, studios and shops, analyse and present findings, and write a report with introduction, methodology, findings and conclusion. The project begins in Form Three and the report is submitted in Form Four.

sla_method: ICT- based learning and Case Study

sla_references: TET(2023), MUSIC SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Grade IV theory covers scales and key signatures up to four sharps and flats, compound and simple times, and more advanced intervals and terms.
sla_notes_details: Rhythm: simple and compound times (2/4, 3/4, 4/4, 2/2, 3/2, 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8), duplets and triplets, syncopation and the grouping of notes and rests. Scales and key signatures: major and minor keys up to four sharps or flats, including harmonic and melodic minors, and the chromatic scale; alto clef may be included as a further clef in some cases together with treble and bass clefs. Melody and harmony: intervals up to an octave in major, minor, perfect, augmented and diminished forms; the triads of the scale degrees; primary chords I, IV and V and cadences (perfect and imperfect); transposition. Terms and signs: those of earlier grades plus alla marcia, cantabile, grazioso, maestoso, pesante, tranquillo, and ornaments including acciaccatura, appoggiatura, mordent and turn. Learners also analyse short melodies and identify features.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a perfect cadence, chord V followed by chord I, ends a phrase in the key of C with the chords G and C.
sla_notes_daily_life: Advanced theory helps choir directors, teachers and composers to arrange and analyse music.
sla_exercise: Which chords make a perfect cadence?::V followed by I.||How many sharps has the key of E major?::Four.||What does cantabile mean?::In a singing style.

sla_references: TET(2023), MUSIC SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Three-part harmony has three independent voice lines that combine to form full chords.
sla_notes_details: Learners write lyrics in any language and a melody in a suitable key, then add two lower lines using chord notes of I, IV and V in root position and inversions. Typical voicings are soprano-alto-tenor or soprano-alto-bass. Good voice leading: move smoothly by step, avoid parallel fifths and octaves, keep parts within their comfortable range, and end with a perfect cadence. Balance the parts rhythmically, use imitation or contrast, and mark dynamics and tempo. Software can play back each line for checking.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, over a C major chord the soprano sings G, the alto E and the tenor C, making a complete triad.
sla_notes_daily_life: Three-part songs are used by school choirs and church groups to enrich their sound.
sla_exercise: Which chord tones form a C major triad?::C, E and G.||Name one rule of good voice leading.::Avoid parallel fifths and octaves (or move smoothly by step).||How should a composition end?::On the tonic chord, usually after a perfect cadence.

sla_references: TET(2023), MUSIC SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Four-part harmony (SATB) uses soprano, alto, tenor and bass lines to create rich, balanced chords.
sla_notes_details: Composers write lyrics and a melody for the soprano, then supply alto, tenor and bass parts. The bass usually carries the root of the chord, and the inner voices complete the triad, with the root sometimes doubled. Voice ranges must be respected (soprano C4 to G5, alto G3 to D5, tenor C3 to G4, bass E2 to C4). Rules: keep adjacent upper voices within an octave, avoid crossing of voices, avoid parallel fifths and octaves, and use common tones and steps where possible. Chords I, IV, V, vi, and cadences are used. The parts are written on two staves with a soprano-alto stave and a tenor-bass stave.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in C major the chord progression I, IV, V, I gives bass notes C, F, G and C under the soprano melody.
sla_notes_daily_life: Four-part harmony is the standard in mixed choirs, so composing in it prepares learners for choir work.
sla_exercise: Name the four voices in SATB.::Soprano, alto, tenor and bass.||What does the bass part normally sing in a chord?::The root (lowest note) of the chord.||How many staves are usually used to write SATB?::Two staves.

sla_notes_intro: Singing three-part harmony requires each singer to maintain their own line and blend with the other two.
sla_notes_details: The choir is divided into three groups, for example soprano, alto and tenor or soprano, alto and bass. Each part is learned separately with a piano or recorded guide, then two parts are combined, then all three. Learners are trained to tune intervals, breathe at the same points and balance the parts. Dynamics, phrasing, and diction are worked out in rehearsals in student music clubs. Performance requires a conductor and correct posture. Recording of the rehearsals helps self-assessment.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the choir first learns the alto line alone, then sings it with the soprano, and finally adds the bass.
sla_notes_daily_life: Choirs in schools and churches perform three-part songs during services and competitions.
sla_exercise: How are three-part songs rehearsed?::Each part is learned separately then combined gradually.||Why is a recording useful during rehearsal?::It allows singers to check their pitch and balance.||Name three voice parts that can form a three-part choir.::Soprano, alto and bass (or soprano, alto and tenor).

sla_notes_intro: Four-part singing brings together soprano, alto, tenor and bass lines in a full choral sound.
sla_notes_details: Rehearsal begins with vocal warm-ups and tuning, then each section learns its part, first with an instrument and then without. Sections are combined gradually: soprano and bass first, then alto and tenor. Singers are trained to match vowels, control dynamics, and maintain balance so that the melody is audible. Diction, breathing at agreed places, and following the conductor's beat are stressed. Student music clubs organise regular practice, and performances are evaluated for intonation, blend and expression.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a school choir sings a four-part hymn where the basses provide a firm foundation and the sopranos carry the tune.
sla_notes_daily_life: Four-part choral music is heard at graduations, concerts, church services and national events.
sla_exercise: Which two parts are usually combined first when rehearsing SATB?::Soprano and bass.||What does blend mean in choral singing?::Voices sound together as one balanced tone.||Why must singers follow the conductor?::To keep the same tempo, entries and dynamics.

sla_notes_intro: Wind instruments produce sound when air vibrates inside a tube, and they include woodwind and brass instruments.
sla_notes_details: Local examples are baragumu (horns), filimbi (flutes and whistles), zumari and panpipes; foreign examples are the recorder, flute, clarinet, saxophone, trumpet, trombone and French horn. Sound is produced by blowing across an edge (flute), through a reed (clarinet, saxophone) or by buzzing lips into a mouthpiece (trumpet). Pitch is changed by covering holes, using valves or a slide. Learners study breath control, embouchure, fingering, simple scales and short melodies for accompaniment, and care such as cleaning and drying. They accompany songs by playing countermelodies, sustained chords or the tune.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a learner plays the recorder melody an octave higher than the singers while the class sings a short song.
sla_notes_daily_life: Wind instruments are used in brass bands, school bands, church bands and traditional ceremonies.
sla_exercise: Name two local wind instruments.::Baragumu and filimbi.||How is sound produced on a trumpet?::By buzzing the lips into the mouthpiece so the air column vibrates.||Give one way of caring for a wind instrument.::Clean and dry it after playing.

They enter the melody and accompaniment on separate staves, adding chords, dynamics, articulation, lyrics and repeat marks, then use playback, mixer and parts functions to check. sla_notes_intro: Setting up a music production business needs planning, registration, capital, equipment and marketing.
sla_notes_details: Steps are: identify a market need and write a business plan; determine capital and sources such as savings, loans and grants; choose a suitable location; register the business with BRELA and get a tax number from TRA and licences from BASATA and local government; acquire equipment (computer, DAW, microphones, interface, monitors) and soundproof the room; hire staff or freelancers; set prices; sign contracts with clients and respect copyright through COSOTA; market services; keep accounts; and plan for growth. sla_notes_intro: Online marketing uses digital channels for distributing, selling and promoting music, and includes attention to royalties and pricing.
sla_notes_details: Distribution: uploading songs to streaming platforms such as Boomplay, Audiomack, Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube and using aggregators; ring-back tones through mobile networks; and digital downloads. Royalties: payments made to creators each time a work is streamed, downloaded, broadcast or performed, collected by COSOTA and platforms; artists should register their works and keep contracts. Pricing: set by the artist or label based on costs, audience income and competition; strategies include free samples, subscription bundles, pay-per-download and event ticketing. Other strategies are email lists, websites, social media campaigns and collaborations. Keep records and analyse data.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, an artist releases a single on Boomplay and YouTube, earns from streams, and receives performance royalties through COSOTA.
sla_notes_daily_life: Online platforms let a musician in a small town reach fans across the country and abroad.
sla_exercise: What is a royalty?::A payment made to creators for the use of their music.||Name two platforms for distributing music online.::Boomplay and YouTube (also Audiomack, Spotify).||Give one factor used when pricing music.::Cost of production and the income level of the audience (or competition).

main_competence_name: Carry out a project in Music
specific_competence_name: Conduct a research project on business opportunities in music
learning_activity_name: Complete and submit a report on the research project started in Form Three
sla_name: Completing and submitting the music business research report
sla_assessment_criteria: A report on the research project started in Form Three is completed and submitted successfully.
sla_teaching_aids: Videos related to successful music business ventures|Industry reports|Market research
sla_references: TET(2023), MUSIC SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The final report presents the findings of the research project begun in Form Three.
sla_notes_details: Learners complete data analysis using tables, graphs and summaries, interpret the results in relation to the objectives, and write the report with a title page, introduction, objectives, methodology, findings, discussion, conclusion, recommendations, references and appendices. Language must be clear and correct, ethics observed, sources acknowledged and plagiarism avoided. The report is edited, proofread, presented to the class or panel, and submitted on time. Learners reflect on lessons learned and challenges.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a report may show that 60 percent of interviewed artists earn income from live shows and recommends creating more performance venues.
sla_notes_daily_life: Report writing skills are useful in later studies, work and running small businesses.
sla_exercise: Name two parts of a research report.::Introduction and conclusion (also methodology, findings).||Why should sources be acknowledged?::To avoid plagiarism and give credit to the owners.||What can be used to present numerical findings?::Tables and graphs.
